title: The Diner
content: I'm curious if anyone's ever been to my special MallWorld place. I hope you have! It's awesome! I've spent days driving around, trying to find it in real life. It's somewhere in the midwestern U.S. It's in a wooded area at an intersection with stop signs. There's nothing out-of-place or remote about the diner - you know the suburbs are only a few minutes away - it just happens to be the only bit of development right here. There might be a state forest preserve keeping the area from being too developed. The parking lot is spacious and well-lit. There are a few other cars in the lot. It's winter. You can see your breath and your feet crunch the snow - already more-or-less packed down from others' footsteps - as you walk in. It's got two sets of swinging doors like lots of restaurants do, to keep out the cold. The little vestibule between the two has the weird industrial rug where you stamp the snow off your shoes, wet from everybody who came before you. There's a bulletin board in the vestibule. Rooms for rent, petsitters, notices about local church potlucks, stuff like that. The diner isn't a franchise or a chain. It's its only location. It's decent-sized, well-lit. When you walk in, you're looking at the cashier/host stand. It's got the spinning carousel-tower of pies off to your immediate right. The entrance is in the corner of the diner, so the walls of booths stretch ahead and to your right; the windows on the wall to your right look out onto the parking lot. A few other customers at the booths and tables. You came to the diner by yourself, but sometimes Noah happens to be there. Noah is a tall, thin, youngish guy. Blonde hair, affable. He looks a bit like Evan Peters, the actor, but with a softer/happier, hippie-ish vibe. He might be swimming in an oversized rumpled hoodie. You recognize him and you think you know him, but you might be wrong, you don't say hi to him first because you might be mistaken and you don't want to be rude, but he's so happy to see you, and he remembers everything. You've taken off your coat. "Coffee, hon?" the waitress asks as you're piling the coat next to you in the long booth. Personally, I answer in the affirmative. But as you settle into your booth, you have this moment of clarity. You realize that everything that had ever happened to you, in your whole life, was good and right, because it brought you to this place. You realize that everything is going to make sense now. The struggle is over, and it's not that you've won, but the rules of the game have changed around you. You fit your life, now, in a way you never did before, and it was this place that made it happen.
